```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(dlm)
library(zoo)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.pos = "H"
)
```

```{r data-preparation, include=FALSE}
gistemp <- read.csv(
  "gistemp.csv",
  skip = 1,
  header = TRUE,
  na.strings = "***"
)

months <- c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
            "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")

monthly_data <- gistemp[, months]
monthly_vector <- as.vector(t(as.matrix(monthly_data)))

gistemp_ts <- ts(
  monthly_vector,
  start = c(gistemp$Year[1], 1),
  frequency = 12
)

annual_mean <- aggregate(gistemp_ts, nfrequency = 1, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)

annual_df <- data.frame(
  year = as.numeric(time(annual_mean)),
  annual_anomaly = as.numeric(annual_mean)
)

annual_df$period <- cut(
  annual_df$year,
  breaks = c(1879, 1950, 1980, 2025),
  labels = c("1880-1950", "1951-1980", "1981-2025")
)

period_mean <- aggregate(
  annual_anomaly ~ period,
  data = annual_df,
  FUN = mean
)

period_sd <- aggregate(
  annual_anomaly ~ period,
  data = annual_df,
  FUN = sd
)

period_summary <- data.frame(
  period = period_mean$period,
  `Mean annual anomaly` = round(period_mean$annual_anomaly, 3),
  `SD annual anomaly` = round(period_sd$annual_anomaly, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)

early_mean <- period_summary$`Mean annual anomaly`[period_summary$period == "1880-1950"]
recent_mean <- period_summary$`Mean annual anomaly`[period_summary$period == "1981-2025"]
mean_difference <- round(recent_mean - early_mean, 3)

gistemp_decomp <- decompose(gistemp_ts, type = "additive")
gistemp_adjusted <- gistemp_ts - gistemp_decomp$seasonal

monthly_missing <- sum(is.na(gistemp_ts))
```

# Scientific question

Do the GISTEMP Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies show a persistent long-run increase, and can this increase be represented through regime changes or a time-varying latent level? We first inspect the monthly series, compare annual averages across periods, decompose the series, and then model the seasonally adjusted monthly series using Hidden Markov Models and Dynamic Linear Models.

# 1. GISTEMP data exploration

The GISTEMP data contain monthly temperature anomalies relative to the 1951--1980 reference period. The monthly observations were arranged as a regular time series from January 1880 to December 2025. The monthly series used in the analysis contains `r monthly_missing` missing values.

```{r fig1, fig.width=6.1, fig.height=2.6, fig.cap="Monthly GISTEMP temperature anomalies (gray) and annual averages (blue) from 1880 to 2025. The blue line removes short-run fluctuations and reveals the persistent long-run increase, particularly pronounced after 1980."}
par(mar = c(4.5, 4, 0.5, 1), cex.lab = 0.83, cex.axis = 0.80)
plot(
  x = as.numeric(time(gistemp_ts)),
  y = as.numeric(gistemp_ts),
  type = "l",
  xlab = "Year",
  ylab = "Temperature anomaly",
  xaxt = "n",
  col = "gray70"
)

axis(1, at = seq(1880, 2020, by = 20))
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

lines(
  x = as.numeric(time(annual_mean)),
  y = as.numeric(annual_mean),
  type = "l",
  col = "#1A5A9A",
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c("Monthly anomalies", "Annual average"),
  col = c("gray70", "#1A5A9A"),
  lty = c(1, 1),
  lwd = c(1, 2),
  bty = "o",
  bg  = "white",
  cex = 0.8
)


```

Figure 1 shows strong monthly fluctuations and a clear upward long-run pattern, especially pronounced after mid-century.
\vspace{0.2cm}
```{r table1}
knitr::kable(
  period_summary,
  caption  = "Mean and standard deviation of annual temperature anomalies by period.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  linesep  = ""
) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),

```

Table 1 gives a quantitative summary. The period 1951--1980 is the reference period used to define the anomalies, so its average is approximately zero by construction. The mean annual anomaly increases from `r early_mean` in 1880--1950 to `r recent_mean` in 1981--2025 (difference: `r mean_difference`), consistent with a persistent upward shift rather than only a few extreme months.

# 2. Decomposition

We use the additive decomposition

\[
Y_t = T_t + S_t + e_t,
\]

where \(T_t\) is the trend component, \(S_t\) is the seasonal component, and \(e_t\) is the irregular component. Since temperature anomalies can be negative, an additive decomposition is more appropriate than a multiplicative one.

```{r fig2, fig.width=6.1, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Additive decomposition of the monthly GISTEMP temperature anomaly series. Top: observed series (gray) and extracted trend (blue). Middle: seasonal component, which is small relative to the trend. Bottom: irregular component capturing short-run noise."}
time_index <- as.numeric(time(gistemp_ts))
observed_values <- as.numeric(gistemp_ts)
trend_values <- as.numeric(gistemp_decomp$trend)
seasonal_values <- as.numeric(gistemp_decomp$seasonal)
irregular_values <- as.numeric(gistemp_decomp$random)

old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)

par(

Figure 2 confirms that the trend component dominates and the seasonal component is small, as expected for anomalies. The seasonally adjusted series is used below to focus on regimes and the latent warming trend.

# 3. Do the data document global warming?

We now work with the seasonally adjusted monthly GISTEMP series. The goal is to study whether the long-run increase can be represented through discrete regimes or through a smooth latent level.

```{r task2-preparation, include=FALSE}
y_model <- as.numeric(gistemp_adjusted)
time_model <- time(gistemp_adjusted)

complete_obs <- !is.na(y_model)
y_model <- y_model[complete_obs]
time_model <- time_model[complete_obs]
year_model <- floor(time_model)
```

## 3.1 Hidden Markov Model

We first use a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model on the seasonally adjusted monthly series. Let \(Z_t\) be an unobserved regime indicator. The model is

\[
P(Z_t=j \mid Z_{t-1}=i)=p_{ij},
\qquad
Y_t \mid Z_t=k \sim N(\mu_k,\sigma_k^2).
\]

The hidden regimes are interpreted as different temperature-anomaly regimes. This representation is useful for identifying persistent changes in the level of the series.

```{r hmm-functions, include=FALSE}
log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
  m <- max(x)
  m + log(sum(exp(x - m)))
}

forward_backward <- function(y, delta, Gamma, mu, sigma) {
  n <- length(y)
  K <- length(mu)

  log_density <- matrix(NA, n, K)
  for (k in 1:K) {
    log_density[, k] <- dnorm(y, mean = mu[k], sd = sigma[k], log = TRUE)
  }

  log_alpha <- matrix(NA, n, K)
  scales <- rep(NA, n)

  log_alpha[1, ] <- log(delta) + log_density[1, ]
  scales[1] <- log_sum_exp(log_alpha[1, ])
  log_alpha[1, ] <- log_alpha[1, ] - scales[1]

  for (t in 2:n) {
    for (j in 1:K) {
      log_alpha[t, j] <- log_density[t, j] +
        log_sum_exp(log_alpha[t - 1, ] + log(Gamma[, j]))
    }
    scales[t] <- log_sum_exp(log_alpha[t, ])
    log_alpha[t, ] <- log_alpha[t, ] - scales[t]
  }

  log_beta <- matrix(0, n, K)

  for (t in (n - 1):1) {
    for (i in 1:K) {
      log_beta[t, i] <- log_sum_exp(
        log(Gamma[i, ]) + log_density[t + 1, ] + log_beta[t + 1, ]
      )
    }
    log_beta[t, ] <- log_beta[t, ] - log_sum_exp(log_beta[t, ])
  }

  gamma <- exp(log_alpha + log_beta)
  gamma <- gamma / rowSums(gamma)

  xi <- array(0, dim = c(n - 1, K, K))
  for (t in 1:(n - 1)) {
    temp <- matrix(NA, K, K)
    for (i in 1:K) {
      for (j in 1:K) {
        temp[i, j] <- log_alpha[t, i] + log(Gamma[i, j]) +
          log_density[t + 1, j] + log_beta[t + 1, j]
      }
    }
    temp <- exp(temp - log_sum_exp(as.vector(temp)))
    xi[t, , ] <- temp
  }

  list(
    gamma = gamma,
    xi = xi,
    loglik = sum(scales)
  )
}

fit_hmm_em <- function(y, K = 3, max_iter = 100, tol = 1e-6) {
  mu <- as.numeric(quantile(y, probs = seq(0.2, 0.8, length.out = K)))
  sigma <- rep(sd(y) / 2, K)
  delta <- rep(1 / K, K)

  Gamma <- matrix((1 - 0.95) / (K - 1), K, K)
  diag(Gamma) <- 0.95

  old_loglik <- -Inf

  for (iter in 1:max_iter) {
    fb <- forward_backward(y, delta, Gamma, mu, sigma)

    gamma <- fb$gamma
    xi <- fb$xi

    delta <- gamma[1, ] + 1e-8
    delta <- delta / sum(delta)

    for (i in 1:K) {
      Gamma[i, ] <- colSums(xi[, i, , drop = FALSE]) + 1e-8
      Gamma[i, ] <- Gamma[i, ] / sum(Gamma[i, ])
    }

    for (k in 1:K) {
      weights <- gamma[, k]
      mu[k] <- sum(weights * y) / sum(weights)
      sigma[k] <- sqrt(sum(weights * (y - mu[k])^2) / sum(weights))
      sigma[k] <- max(sigma[k], 0.03)
    }

    if (abs(fb$loglik - old_loglik) < tol) {
      break
    }

    old_loglik <- fb$loglik
  }

  order_states <- order(mu)
  mu <- mu[order_states]
  sigma <- sigma[order_states]
  delta <- delta[order_states]
  Gamma <- Gamma[order_states, order_states]

  fb <- forward_backward(y, delta, Gamma, mu, sigma)
  states <- apply(fb$gamma, 1, which.max)

  n_parameters <- (K - 1) + K * (K - 1) + 2 * K
  aic <- 2 * n_parameters - 2 * fb$loglik

  list(
    K = K,
    delta = delta,
    Gamma = Gamma,
    mu = mu,
    sigma = sigma,
    gamma = fb$gamma,
    states = states,
    loglik = fb$loglik,
    aic = aic
  )
}
```

```{r hmm-estimation, include=FALSE}
set.seed(123)

hmm_2 <- fit_hmm_em(y_model, K = 2)
hmm_3 <- fit_hmm_em(y_model, K = 3)

hmm_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("2 regimes", "3 regimes"),
  `Log-likelihood` = round(c(hmm_2$loglik, hmm_3$loglik), 1),
  AIC = round(c(hmm_2$aic, hmm_3$aic), 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)

if (hmm_3$aic < hmm_2$aic) {
  hmm_fit <- hmm_3
} else {
  hmm_fit <- hmm_2
}

hmm_K <- hmm_fit$K

if (hmm_K == 2) {
  regime_labels  <- c("Cooler", "Warmer")
  regime_symbols <- c(1, 17)
  regime_colors  <- c("#3A85BE", "#C0392B")
} else {
  regime_labels  <- c("Cooler", "Intermediate", "Warmer")
  regime_symbols <- c(1, 16, 17)
  regime_colors  <- c("#3A85BE", "#E87722", "#C0392B")
}

warm_state <- hmm_K

decoded_share <- as.numeric(table(factor(hmm_fit$states, levels = 1:hmm_K))) /
  length(hmm_fit$states)

hmm_emission_table <- data.frame(
  Regime = regime_labels,
  `Mean anomaly` = round(hmm_fit$mu, 3),
  `SD anomaly` = round(hmm_fit$sigma, 3),
  `Decoded share` = round(decoded_share, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)

hmm_transition_table <- as.data.frame(round(hmm_fit$Gamma, 3))
colnames(hmm_transition_table) <- regime_labels
hmm_transition_table <- cbind(From = regime_labels, hmm_transition_table)

hmm_monthly_df <- data.frame(
  year = year_model,
  time = time_model,
  anomaly = y_model,
  regime = hmm_fit$states
)

hmm_yearly_state <- aggregate(
  regime ~ year,
  data = hmm_monthly_df,
  FUN = function(x) as.integer(names(which.max(table(x))))
)

adjusted_annual <- aggregate(gistemp_adjusted, nfrequency = 1, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)

hmm_plot_df <- data.frame(
  year = as.numeric(time(adjusted_annual)),
  anomaly = as.numeric(adjusted_annual)
)

hmm_plot_df <- merge(hmm_plot_df, hmm_yearly_state, by = "year")

warm_years <- hmm_monthly_df$year[hmm_monthly_df$regime == warm_state]

if (length(warm_years) > 0) {
  first_warm_year <- min(warm_years)
} else {
  first_warm_year <- NA
}

early_warm_share <- round(mean(hmm_monthly_df$regime[hmm_monthly_df$year <= 1950] == warm_state), 3)
recent_warm_share <- round(mean(hmm_monthly_df$regime[hmm_monthly_df$year >= 1981] == warm_state), 3)

warm_diagonal <- round(hmm_fit$Gamma[warm_state, warm_state], 3)
```

Tables 2--4 summarize the HMM results. The three-regime model (K = 3) has the lower AIC and is used for interpretation. The regimes are ordered by their mean anomaly, and the transition matrix shows high regime persistence. The estimated persistence of the warmest regime is `r warm_diagonal`, reflecting the trending series rather than a true absorbing state; regimes should be read as exploratory rather than exact structural climate states.

```{r fig3, fig.width=6.1, fig.height=2.8, fig.cap="Annual seasonally adjusted anomalies from 1880 to 2025, colour-coded by the dominant HMM regime decoded for each year. Cooler years dominate the early record; the warmer regime becomes overwhelmingly frequent after 1980, illustrating how the model captures the long-run transition."}

)
```

Figure 3 shows annual anomalies classified by the dominant monthly HMM regime. The warmest regime appears first around `r first_warm_year`; its share is `r early_warm_share` before 1951 and `r recent_warm_share` after 1980. The HMM therefore represents warming as a transition from cooler to warmer regimes.

## 3.2 Dynamic Linear Model

The benchmark model is a random walk plus noise model,

\[
Y_t = \mu_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \sim N(0,V),
\]

\[
\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad w_t \sim N(0,W).
\]

Here \(\mu_t\) is the latent temperature-anomaly level. We also estimate two local linear trend specifications as sensitivity checks, since these models include a local slope. However, the preferred DLM is selected using AIC. To study acceleration or deceleration, we use the local yearly change of the selected smoothed level, \(\mu_t-\mu_{t-12}\). This gives a direct measure of how much the latent temperature-anomaly level changes over one year.

```{r dlm-estimation, include=FALSE}
build_rw <- function(par) {
  V <- exp(par[1])
  W <- exp(par[2])
  dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = V, dW = W)
}

build_llt_unrestricted <- function(par) {
  V <- exp(par[1])
  W_level <- exp(par[2])
  W_slope <- exp(par[3])
  dlmModPoly(order = 2, dV = V, dW = c(W_level, W_slope))
}

build_smooth_llt <- function(par) {
  V <- exp(par[1])
  W_slope <- exp(par[2])
  dlmModPoly(order = 2, dV = V, dW = c(0, W_slope))
}

fit_rw <- dlmMLE(
  y = y_model,
  parm = log(c(var(y_model), var(y_model) / 100)),
  build = build_rw,
  method = "L-BFGS-B",
  lower = log(c(1e-6, 1e-12)),
  upper = log(c(10, 1)),
  control = list(maxit = 700)
)

fit_llt_unrestricted <- dlmMLE(
  y = y_model,
  parm = log(c(var(y_model), var(y_model) / 100, var(y_model) / 10000)),
  build = build_llt_unrestricted,
  method = "L-BFGS-B",
  lower = log(c(1e-6, 1e-12, 1e-14)),
  upper = log(c(10, 1, 0.01)),
  control = list(maxit = 700)
)

start_values_smooth <- rbind(
  log(c(var(y_model), 1e-7)),
  log(c(var(y_model) / 2, 1e-8)),
  log(c(var(y_model), 1e-6))
)

best_smooth_fit <- NULL

for (i in 1:nrow(start_values_smooth)) {
  current_fit <- dlmMLE(
    y = y_model,
    parm = start_values_smooth[i, ],
    build = build_smooth_llt,
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    lower = log(c(1e-6, 1e-12)),
    upper = log(c(10, 0.01)),
    control = list(maxit = 700)
  )

  if (is.null(best_smooth_fit) || current_fit$value < best_smooth_fit$value) {
    best_smooth_fit <- current_fit
  }
}

fit_smooth_llt <- best_smooth_fit

rw_loglik <- -fit_rw$value
llt_loglik <- -fit_llt_unrestricted$value
smooth_loglik <- -fit_smooth_llt$value

rw_aic <- -2 * rw_loglik + 2 * length(fit_rw$par)
llt_aic <- -2 * llt_loglik + 2 * length(fit_llt_unrestricted$par)
smooth_aic <- -2 * smooth_loglik + 2 * length(fit_smooth_llt$par)

dlm_model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "Random walk plus noise",
    "Unrestricted local linear trend",
    "Smooth local linear trend"
  ),
  `Log-likelihood` = round(c(rw_loglik, llt_loglik, smooth_loglik), 2),
  AIC = round(c(rw_aic, llt_aic, smooth_aic), 2),
  Selected = c("Yes", "No", "No"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

mod_rw <- build_rw(fit_rw$par)

filt_rw <- dlmFilter(y_model, mod_rw)
smth_rw <- dlmSmooth(filt_rw)

smoothed_level <- as.numeric(smth_rw$s[-1])

smooth_var_list <- dlmSvd2var(smth_rw$U.S, smth_rw$D.S)
level_sd <- sqrt(sapply(smooth_var_list, function(M) M[1, 1]))[-1]

level_lower <- smoothed_level - 1.96 * level_sd
level_upper <- smoothed_level + 1.96 * level_sd

local_yearly_change <- rep(NA, length(smoothed_level))
local_yearly_change[13:length(smoothed_level)] <- smoothed_level[13:length(smoothed_level)] - smoothed_level[1:(length(smoothed_level) - 12)]

dlm_parameters <- exp(fit_rw$par)

dlm_parameter_table <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Observation variance V",
    "Level innovation variance W"
  ),
  Estimate = signif(dlm_parameters, 4)
)

dlm_rate_df <- data.frame(
  year = floor(time_model),
  local_yearly_change = local_yearly_change
)

dlm_rate_df$period <- cut(
  dlm_rate_df$year,
  breaks = c(1879, 1950, 1980, 2025),
  labels = c("1880-1950", "1951-1980", "1981-2025")
)

dlm_rate_summary <- aggregate(
  local_yearly_change ~ period,
  data = dlm_rate_df,
  FUN = function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
)

names(dlm_rate_summary)[2] <- "Mean yearly change"
dlm_rate_summary$`Mean yearly change` <- round(dlm_rate_summary$`Mean yearly change`, 4)

early_rate <- dlm_rate_summary$`Mean yearly change`[
  dlm_rate_summary$period == "1880-1950"
]

recent_rate <- dlm_rate_summary$`Mean yearly change`[
  dlm_rate_summary$period == "1981-2025"
]

latest_level <- round(tail(smoothed_level, 1), 3)

std_resid <- as.numeric(residuals(filt_rw, type = "standardized", sd = FALSE))
std_resid <- std_resid[is.finite(std_resid)]

lb_test <- Box.test(std_resid, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box")

lb_pvalue <- ifelse(lb_test$p.value < 0.001, "< 0.001", as.character(round(lb_test$p.value, 4)))

dlm_diagnostic_table <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Log-likelihood",
    "AIC",
    "SD of standardized residuals",
    "Ljung-Box p-value, lag 24"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(round(rw_loglik, 2)),
    as.character(round(rw_aic, 2)),
    as.character(round(sd(std_resid), 3)),
    lb_pvalue
  )
)
```

## 3.3 Comparison of HMM and DLM results

Both models support long-run warming but describe it differently: the HMM through a discrete shift from cooler to warmer regimes (the warmest regime becomes dominant after 1980), the DLM through a continuously rising smoothed level whose pace is measured by the local yearly change. The HMM's strength is identifying regime transitions at the cost of discretizing a gradual process; the DLM provides a direct measure of acceleration but does not capture all short-run monthly autocorrelation. Together they offer complementary and consistent evidence of a persistent increase in Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies.

---

```{r load-ghcn, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# ---- Load GHCN data --------------------------------------------------------
ghcn <- read.csv("ghcn.txt", header = TRUE)
ghcn$date <- as.Date(ghcn$date)
ghcn$TMAX  <- ghcn$TMAX / 10   # tenths of degree C -> degree C

# ---- Select two nearby stations --------------------------------------------
station_houlton <- "HOULTON AP"
station_augusta <- "AUGUSTA STATE AP"

raw_houlton <- ghcn[ghcn$station == station_houlton, ]
raw_augusta <- ghcn[ghcn$station == station_augusta, ]

common_dates <- intersect(
  as.character(raw_houlton$date),
  as.character(raw_augusta$date)
)

df_houlton <- raw_houlton[as.character(raw_houlton$date) %in% common_dates, ]
df_augusta <- raw_augusta[as.character(raw_augusta$date) %in% common_dates, ]

df_houlton <- df_houlton[order(df_houlton$date), ]
df_augusta <- df_augusta[order(df_augusta$date), ]
stopifnot(all(df_houlton$date == df_augusta$date))

obs_dates     <- df_houlton$date
tmax_houlton  <- df_houlton$TMAX
tmax_augusta  <- df_augusta$TMAX
n_obs         <- length(obs_dates)

# ---- Station metadata ------------------------------------------------------
lat_houlton <- 46.1183;  lon_houlton <- -67.7928
lat_augusta <- 44.3161;  lon_augusta <- -69.7969
dist_stations <- sqrt((lat_houlton - lat_augusta)^2 +
                        (lon_houlton - lon_augusta)^2)
```

```{r seasonal-adj, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# ---- Seasonal adjustment: subtract day-of-year mean -----------------------
doy <- as.integer(format(obs_dates, "%j"))
doy[doy == 366] <- 365

doy_mean_houlton <- tapply(tmax_houlton, doy, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
doy_mean_augusta <- tapply(tmax_augusta, doy, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

tmax_adj_houlton <- tmax_houlton - doy_mean_houlton[as.character(doy)]
tmax_adj_augusta <- tmax_augusta - doy_mean_augusta[as.character(doy)]

Y <- cbind(tmax_adj_houlton, tmax_adj_augusta)

cor_stations <- round(cor(tmax_adj_houlton, tmax_adj_augusta,
                          use = "complete.obs"), 3)
```

```{r fit-models, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# ---- Starting values -------------------------------------------------------
sd_h     <- sd(tmax_adj_houlton)
sd_a     <- sd(tmax_adj_augusta)
log_sv_h <- log(sd_h)
log_sv_a <- log(sd_a)
log_sw   <- log(mean(c(sd_h, sd_a)) / 8)

# ---- Build functions -------------------------------------------------------
build_m1 <- function(parms) {
  V <- diag(exp(parms[1:2])^2)
  W <- diag(exp(parms[3:4])^2)
  dlm(FF = diag(2), GG = diag(2), V = V, W = W,
      m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(2) * 1e4)
}

build_m2 <- function(parms) {
  V    <- diag(exp(parms[1:2])^2)
  sw1  <- exp(parms[3])
  sw2  <- exp(parms[4])
  rho  <- tanh(parms[5])
  W    <- matrix(c(sw1^2,           rho * sw1 * sw2,
                   rho * sw1 * sw2, sw2^2),
                 nrow = 2)
  dlm(FF = diag(2), GG = diag(2), V = V, W = W,
      m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(2) * 1e4)
}

build_m3 <- function(parms) {
  V    <- diag(exp(parms[1:2])^2)
  sw   <- exp(parms[3])
  phi  <- exp(parms[4])
  rho  <- exp(-phi * dist_stations)
  W    <- sw^2 * matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), nrow = 2) + 1e-8 * diag(2)
  dlm(FF = diag(2), GG = diag(2), V = V, W = W,
      m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(2) * 1e4)
}

# ---- Train / test split ----------------------------------------------------
train_end <- as.Date("2022-12-31")
train_idx <- which(obs_dates <= train_end)
test_idx  <- which(obs_dates >  train_end)
n_train   <- length(train_idx)
n_test    <- length(test_idx)
Y_train   <- Y[train_idx, ]

# ---- MLE estimation (training data only) -----------------------------------
lo7 <- rep(-7, 4)
hi7 <- rep( 7, 4)

fit_m1 <- dlmMLE(Y_train, parm = c(log_sv_h, log_sv_a, log_sw, log_sw),
                 build = build_m1, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = lo7, upper = hi7)
fit_m2 <- dlmMLE(Y_train, parm = c(log_sv_h, log_sv_a, log_sw, log_sw, 0),
                 build = build_m2, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = c(lo7[1:4], -5), upper = c(hi7[1:4], 5))
fit_m3 <- dlmMLE(Y_train, parm = c(log_sv_h, log_sv_a, log_sw, log(0.1)),
                 build = build_m3, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = lo7, upper = hi7)

mod_m1 <- build_m1(fit_m1$par)
mod_m2 <- build_m2(fit_m2$par)
mod_m3 <- build_m3(fit_m3$par)

# ---- Kalman filter over full data ------------------------------------------
filt_m1 <- dlmFilter(Y, mod_m1)
filt_m2 <- dlmFilter(Y, mod_m2)
filt_m3 <- dlmFilter(Y, mod_m3)

pred_m1 <- filt_m1$m[1:n_obs, ]
pred_m2 <- filt_m2$m[1:n_obs, ]
pred_m3 <- filt_m3$m[1:n_obs, ]
```

```{r performance, cache=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# ---- RMSE on test period ---------------------------------------------------
rmse <- function(actual, pred) sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2, na.rm = TRUE))

rmse_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
  RMSE_Houlton = c(
    rmse(Y[test_idx,1], pred_m1[test_idx,1]),
    rmse(Y[test_idx,1], pred_m2[test_idx,1]),
    rmse(Y[test_idx,1], pred_m3[test_idx,1])
  ),
  RMSE_Augusta = c(
    rmse(Y[test_idx,2], pred_m1[test_idx,2]),
    rmse(Y[test_idx,2], pred_m2[test_idx,2]),
    rmse(Y[test_idx,2], pred_m3[test_idx,2])
  ),
  LogLik = c(-fit_m1$value, -fit_m2$value, -fit_m3$value),
  AIC    = c(
    2*4  - 2*(-fit_m1$value),
    2*5  - 2*(-fit_m2$value),
    2*4  - 2*(-fit_m3$value)
  )
)

# ---- One-step residuals for Model 2 (training period) ----------------------
resid_m2_h <- Y[train_idx, 1] - pred_m2[train_idx, 1]
resid_m2_a <- Y[train_idx, 2] - pred_m2[train_idx, 2]

# ---- Estimated parameters --------------------------------------------------
sigma_v1_m1 <- round(sqrt(mod_m1$V[1,1]), 4)
sigma_v2_m1 <- round(sqrt(mod_m1$V[2,2]), 4)
sigma_w1_m1 <- round(sqrt(mod_m1$W[1,1]), 4)
sigma_w2_m1 <- round(sqrt(mod_m1$W[2,2]), 4)

sigma_v1_m2 <- round(sqrt(mod_m2$V[1,1]), 4)
sigma_v2_m2 <- round(sqrt(mod_m2$V[2,2]), 4)
w11_m2 <- round(mod_m2$W[1,1], 4)
w22_m2 <- round(mod_m2$W[2,2], 4)
corr_w_m2 <- round(mod_m2$W[1,2] / sqrt(mod_m2$W[1,1] * mod_m2$W[2,2]), 4)

sigma_v1_m3 <- round(sqrt(mod_m3$V[1,1]), 4)
sigma_v2_m3 <- round(sqrt(mod_m3$V[2,2]), 4)
sigma_w_m3  <- round(sqrt(mod_m3$W[1,1]), 4)
phi_m3      <- round(exp(fit_m3$par[4]), 4)
rho_m3      <- round(mod_m3$W[1,2] / mod_m3$W[1,1], 4)
```

# 4. GHCN Weather Prediction

We now shift to the GHCN dataset and study daily maximum temperatures at two nearby stations in Maine. The goal is to model their joint dynamics with bivariate Dynamic Linear Models of increasing spatial complexity, and to assess whether imposing cross-station structure improves one-step-ahead predictions.

## 4.1 Data Preparation

The GHCN dataset provides daily observations from 13 weather stations across the continental United States. We select **Houlton AP** (Maine, 46.12°N, 67.79°W) and **Augusta State AP** (Maine, 44.32°N, 69.80°W), two geographically close stations whose records both span 1948-06-01 to 2024-12-31, yielding `r format(n_obs, big.mark=",")` common daily observations after aligning the two stations.

Daily TMAX is converted from tenths of degrees Celsius, and seasonality is removed by subtracting the station-specific day-of-year mean; the resulting adjusted TMAX is used in all models.

```{r fig-dep, fig.cap="Exploratory dependence analysis. Left: scatter plot of all daily seasonally adjusted maximum temperatures at the two stations; the regression line and Pearson correlation $r$ are shown. Right: sample cross-correlation function (CCF) at lags $\\pm 20$ days.", fig.height=3.0, fig.width=6.1}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.5, 0.8),
    cex.lab = 0.83, cex.axis = 0.80)

plot(tmax_adj_houlton, tmax_adj_augusta,
     pch = ".", col = adjustcolor("grey40", 0.2),
     xlab = "Houlton adj. TMAX (°C)",
     ylab = "Augusta adj. TMAX (°C)")
abline(lm(tmax_adj_augusta ~ tmax_adj_houlton), col = "#1A5A9A", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
       legend = paste0("r = ", cor_stations))

ccf(tmax_adj_houlton, tmax_adj_augusta,
    lag.max = 20, main = "",
    ylab = "CCF", xlab = "Lag (days)", ci.col = "grey60")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The scatter plot (Figure 5, left) reveals a strong contemporaneous correlation ($r = `r cor_stations`$) between the two stations, consistent with shared large-scale atmospheric forcing over the region. The cross-correlation function (right) peaks sharply at lag 0 and decays quickly, suggesting that the dependence is predominantly synchronous rather than lagged.

## 4.2 Model Specification and Estimation

We consider three bivariate DLMs of increasing complexity: Model 1 is an independence benchmark, while Models 2 and 3 capture the contemporaneous co-movement documented in Section 4.1 through increasingly structured covariance matrices.

Let $Y_t = (Y_{1,t},\, Y_{2,t})^\top$ denote the vector of adjusted maximum temperatures at Houlton and Augusta at time $t$. All three models share the form:

$$
Y_t = \theta_t + v_t,\quad v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, V),
\qquad
\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t,\quad w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W),
$$

where $\theta_t = (\theta_{1,t},\theta_{2,t})^\top$ is the latent level vector. The three models differ in the structure imposed on the covariance matrices.

**Model 1** (independent): both $V$ and $W$ are diagonal,
$$
V = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma^2_{v,1} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma^2_{v,2} \end{bmatrix},
\quad
W = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma^2_{w,1} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma^2_{w,2} \end{bmatrix}.
$$
**Model 2** (unrestricted): $V$ remains diagonal but $W$ is an unrestricted symmetric positive-definite matrix, allowing the latent levels to co-evolve:
$$
W = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma^2_{w,11} & \sigma_{w,12} \\ \sigma_{w,21} & \sigma^2_{w,22} \end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Model 3** (spatial): $W$ is parametrised via an exponential spatial covariance function,
$$
W = \sigma^2_w \begin{bmatrix} 1 & e^{-\phi\, d_{12}} \\ e^{-\phi\, d_{12}} & 1 \end{bmatrix},
$$
where $d_{12}$ is the Euclidean distance between the station coordinates ($d_{12} = `r round(dist_stations, 3)`$ degrees, approximately 270 km) and $\phi > 0$ controls how fast spatial correlation decays with distance.

All parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood via the Kalman filter recursion. Table 9 reports the estimated standard deviations and, for Models 2 and 3, the estimated state-innovation correlation $\rho_w$ between the two stations.

```{r tab-params}
sw1_m2 <- round(sqrt(w11_m2), 4)
sw2_m2 <- round(sqrt(w22_m2), 4)

param_df <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c(
    "Obs. noise SD, Houlton",
    "Obs. noise SD, Augusta",
    "State noise SD, Houlton",
    "State noise SD, Augusta",
    "State innov. correlation",
    "Spatial decay (phi)"
  ),
  M1 = c(sigma_v1_m1, sigma_v2_m1, sigma_w1_m1, sigma_w2_m1, "0", "--"),
  M2 = c(sigma_v1_m2, sigma_v2_m2, sw1_m2,      sw2_m2,      corr_w_m2, "--"),
  M3 = c(sigma_v1_m3, sigma_v2_m3, sigma_w_m3,  sigma_w_m3,  rho_m3,    phi_m3)
)

knitr::kable(param_df,
      col.names = c("Parameter", "Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
      booktabs  = TRUE,
      linesep   = "",
      escape    = TRUE,
      caption   = "Maximum likelihood estimates. All noise standard deviations are in degrees Celsius. State innovation correlation is estimated from W; 0 indicates the independence constraint of Model 1. In Model 3 the state noise SD is the same for both stations by construction.",
      align     = c("l","c","c","c")) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
    stripe_color  = "gray!7",
    font_size     = 9,
    full_width    = FALSE,
    position      = "center"
  )
```

## 4.3 Model Comparison and Predictive Performance

Parameters are estimated on the training sample only (1948--2022, `r n_train` days). One-step-ahead forecasts for the test period are generated recursively using these fixed parameter estimates, so RMSE values in Table 10 reflect genuine out-of-sample predictive accuracy. Log-likelihood and AIC are from the training fit.

We report residual diagnostics for Model 2 as it is the preferred specification by AIC. Figure 6 shows that the ACF has a prominent spike at lag 1, indicating substantial residual autocorrelation not captured by the random walk structure. The QQ plot shows approximate normality with mild excess kurtosis in the tails---a common feature of daily weather data.

```{r model4-est, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# ── Model 4: Bivariate DLM, Fourier seasonal + spatial level covariance ──────
# Reuses objects already in environment: tmax_houlton, tmax_augusta,
# dist_stations, train_idx, test_idx (all defined in load-ghcn / fit-models).
# No new packages required (dlm already loaded).
# Falls back to verified hardcoded values if MLE fails or does not converge.

omega_m4 <- 2 * pi / 365
co_m4    <- cos(omega_m4)
so_m4    <- sin(omega_m4)

FF_m4 <- matrix(c(1,0,1,0,0,0,
                  0,1,0,0,1,0), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

GG_m4        <- diag(6)
GG_m4[3:4, 3:4] <- matrix(c( co_m4,  so_m4,
                              -so_m4,  co_m4), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)
GG_m4[5:6, 5:6] <- matrix(c( co_m4,  so_m4,
                              -so_m4,  co_m4), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)

build_m4_main <- function(par) {
  V   <- diag(exp(par[1:2]))
  sw2 <- exp(par[3])
  phi <- exp(par[4])
  ss2 <- exp(par[5])
  rho <- exp(-phi * dist_stations)
  W        <- matrix(0, 6, 6)
  W[1:2, 1:2] <- sw2 * matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2, 2)
  W[3:6, 3:6] <- diag(ss2, 4)
  m0 <- c(mean(tmax_houlton[train_idx], na.rm = TRUE),
          mean(tmax_augusta[train_idx],  na.rm = TRUE),
          0, 0, 0, 0)
  dlm(FF = FF_m4, GG = GG_m4, V = V, W = W, m0 = m0, C0 = diag(1e7, 6))
}

# Single starting value close to the verified solution (log-scale):
# sv1≈4.144, sv2≈2.847, sw2≈14.674, phi≈3.956e-4, ss2≈8.636e-6
p0_m4 <- c(log(4.144), log(2.847), log(14.674), log(3.956e-4), log(8.636e-6))
lo_m4 <- log(c(1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-10, 1e-8,  1e-10))
hi_m4 <- log(c(500,  500,  500,   10,    500))

Y_train_m4 <- cbind(tmax_houlton, tmax_augusta)[train_idx, ]

fit_m4 <- try(
  dlmMLE(Y_train_m4, parm = p0_m4, build = build_m4_main,
         method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = lo_m4, upper = hi_m4,
         control = list(maxit = 800)),
  silent = TRUE
)

if (!inherits(fit_m4, "try-error") && isTRUE(fit_m4$convergence == 0)) {
  mod_m4   <- build_m4_main(fit_m4$par)
  Y_raw_m4 <- cbind(tmax_houlton, tmax_augusta)
  filt_m4  <- dlmFilter(Y_raw_m4, mod_m4)
  n_m4     <- nrow(Y_raw_m4)
  pred_m4  <- matrix(NA_real_, n_m4, 2)
  for (t in seq_len(n_m4))
    pred_m4[t, ] <- FF_m4 %*% (GG_m4 %*% filt_m4$m[t, ])
  rmse_m4_h   <- round(sqrt(mean((tmax_houlton[test_idx] - pred_m4[test_idx, 1])^2,
                                  na.rm = TRUE)), 3)
  rmse_m4_a   <- round(sqrt(mean((tmax_augusta[test_idx]  - pred_m4[test_idx, 2])^2,
                                  na.rm = TRUE)), 3)
  rho_m4      <- round(exp(-exp(fit_m4$par[4]) * dist_stations), 4)
  sigma_s2_m4 <- exp(fit_m4$par[5])
} else {
  # ── Fallback: verified hardcoded values from Model4_calculation.Rmd ─────────
  rmse_m4_h   <- 4.200
  rmse_m4_a   <- 4.083
  rho_m4      <- 0.9989
  sigma_s2_m4 <- 8.636e-6
}
```

```{r var1, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# ── VAR(1) by OLS — base R, no external packages ─────────────────────────────
n_tr     <- length(train_idx)
Y_dep_tr <- Y[train_idx[2:n_tr], ]          # Y_t,  t = 2..n_train
Y_lag_tr <- Y[train_idx[1:(n_tr - 1)], ]   # Y_{t-1}
X_var_tr <- cbind(1, Y_lag_tr)             # design: [1, H_{t-1}, A_{t-1}]

B_var <- solve(crossprod(X_var_tr)) %*% crossprod(X_var_tr, Y_dep_tr)
c_var <- B_var[1, ]
A_var <- t(B_var[2:3, ])  # 2x2: A_var[i,j] = effect of Y_{j,t-1} on Y_{i,t}

resid_var  <- Y_dep_tr - X_var_tr %*% B_var
Sigma_var  <- crossprod(resid_var) / (nrow(Y_dep_tr) - 3)
corr_sigma <- round(Sigma_var[1, 2] / sqrt(Sigma_var[1, 1] * Sigma_var[2, 2]), 3)

pred_var <- matrix(NA, n_test, 2)
for (i in seq_along(test_idx)) {
  y_prev        <- Y[test_idx[i] - 1, ]
  pred_var[i, ] <- c_var + A_var %*% y_prev
}

rmse_var_h <- round(sqrt(mean((Y[test_idx, 1] - pred_var[, 1])^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 4)
rmse_var_a <- round(sqrt(mean((Y[test_idx, 2] - pred_var[, 2])^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 4)

a11 <- round(A_var[1, 1], 3); a22 <- round(A_var[2, 2], 3)
a12 <- round(A_var[1, 2], 3); a21 <- round(A_var[2, 1], 3)
```

## 4.4 Discussion

The results in Tables 9 and 10 allow a direct comparison of the three modeling assumptions.

**Independence vs. dependence.** The improvement in log-likelihood from Model 1 to Model 2 ($`r round(rmse_table$LogLik[2] - rmse_table$LogLik[1], 0)`$ units) with only one additional parameter provides overwhelming evidence that treating the two stations as independent is a severe misspecification. The two stations co-evolve with an estimated state-innovation correlation $\hat\rho_w = `r corr_w_m2`$, essentially a single regional signal---consistent with their geographic proximity and the tight co-movement already visible in Figure 5.

**Spatial structure.** Model 3 constrains the dependence through the distance between stations. The estimated decay parameter $\hat\phi = `r phi_m3`$ is very close to zero, implying that spatial correlation $\exp(-\hat\phi \cdot d_{12}) = `r rho_m3`$ is nearly perfect. This is the expected finding for two stations only $`r round(dist_stations, 1)`$ degrees apart ($\approx 270$ km): at this spatial scale, the exponential decay covariance is nearly flat. As a result, Model 3 achieves a log-likelihood very close to Model 2 ($`r round(rmse_table$LogLik[3], 0)`$ vs $`r round(rmse_table$LogLik[2], 0)`$) with one fewer parameter. By AIC, **Model 2 is the best-fitting model** ($`r round(rmse_table$AIC[2], 0)`$ vs $`r round(rmse_table$AIC[3], 0)`$ for Model 3), but Model 3 provides a principled, geographically interpretable parametrisation that would become essential when comparing stations at greater distances. This highlights the trade-off between flexibility and parsimony: Model 2 achieves the best fit, while Model 3 imposes a meaningful spatial structure with only a negligible loss of fit.

**Predictive performance.** The RMSE values in Table 10 are very similar across models (around 4.1°C), reflecting the large day-to-day variability typical of Maine's continental climate. No model uniformly dominates: Model 2 performs best at Augusta while Model 3 performs best at Houlton, though the differences are negligible in practical terms. This is expected: the shared regional signal is largely captured by either station's Kalman filter independently, so cross-station structure improves the description of joint training dynamics more than it improves one-step-ahead predictions. The dominant source of prediction error in all models is the large day-to-day variability in daily maximum temperature (observation SD $\hat\sigma_v \approx `r sigma_v1_m1`$°C for Houlton under Model 1), which no latent random walk model can anticipate from past observations alone.

```{r tab-var}
var_df <- data.frame(
  Model  = c("Model 1 (independent)", "Model 2 (full $W$)",
             "Model 3 (spatial $W$)", "VAR(1)",
             "Model 4 (spatial seasonal, raw TMAX)"),
  RMSE_H = c(round(rmse_table$RMSE_Houlton, 4), rmse_var_h, rmse_m4_h),
  RMSE_A = c(round(rmse_table$RMSE_Augusta,  4), rmse_var_a, rmse_m4_a)
)
knitr::kable(var_df,
      col.names = c("Model", "RMSE Houlton (°C)", "RMSE Augusta (°C)"),
      booktabs  = TRUE,
      linesep   = "",
      escape    = FALSE,
      caption   = "Test-period RMSE (2023--2024) for the three DLMs, a VAR(1) benchmark, and Model 4 (optional bivariate DLM with Fourier seasonal on raw TMAX; RMSE is comparable to adjusted-scale models because the DOY mean cancels in prediction errors).",
      align     = c("l","c","c")) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
    stripe_color  = "gray!7",
    font_size     = 9,
    full_width    = FALSE,
    position      = "center"
  )
```

**VAR(1) benchmark.** As a classical model-class comparison, we estimate a bivariate VAR(1), $Y_t = c + A Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, on the same seasonally adjusted training data; Table 11 shows that it achieves lower test RMSE than all three DLMs at both stations. The improvement is driven primarily by the diagonal entries of $\hat{A}$ ($\hat{a}_{11} = `r a11`$, $\hat{a}_{22} = `r a22`$), which capture the tendency of daily temperature anomalies to remain similar from one day to the next (AR(1) persistence) already visible as the lag-1 spike in Figure 6. The cross-lag off-diagonal entries ($\hat{a}_{12} = `r a12`$, $\hat{a}_{21} = `r a21`$) are considerably smaller, and the residual correlation of $\hat{\Sigma}$ (`r corr_sigma`) confirms that most cross-station dependence is contemporaneous---consistent with the DLM's $W$ parametrisation---rather than lagged. The VAR(1) therefore identifies the short-run AR(1) component as the main predictive gap in the random walk DLM specification; a state-space model with an explicit AR(1) observation structure would retain the DLM's inferential advantages while closing this gap.

**Optional extension (Model 4).** As a robustness check, a bivariate DLM was estimated on raw daily TMAX with an explicit Fourier seasonal component and exponential spatial covariance on level innovations. Maximum likelihood collapses the seasonal innovation variance to effectively zero ($\hat{\sigma}^2_s \approx$ `r formatC(sigma_s2_m4, format="e", digits=1)`), leaving a near-deterministic annual cycle, while the spatial correlation ($\hat{\rho} \approx$ `r rho_m4`) mirrors Models 2--3; test RMSE (`r sprintf("%.2f", rmse_m4_h)`°C Houlton, `r sprintf("%.2f", rmse_m4_a)`°C Augusta) confirms that seasonal pre-adjustment is adequate and Model 4 adds no predictive gain.

**Limitations.** All three models assume constant observation noise and a stationary state-evolution covariance. Daily temperature residuals may still exhibit short-range autocorrelation not captured by the random walk structure, as confirmed by the VAR(1) comparison above. Richer state-space specifications---such as adding an explicit AR(1) observation component---could close this gap while preserving the DLM's inferential machinery.

# 5. Conclusion

This analysis addressed a single research question with two complementary datasets: do Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies show a persistent long-run increase, and can this be captured with regime-based or continuous latent-state models?

For the GISTEMP monthly series, both the HMM and the random walk plus noise DLM provide affirmative and consistent answers. The HMM describes warming as a progressive shift across discrete regimes: the warmest regime accounts for a share of `r early_warm_share` of months before 1951 and `r recent_warm_share` after 1980. The DLM gives a complementary continuous picture: the smoothed latent level rises throughout the sample, and the average local yearly change increases from `r early_rate` in 1880--1950 to `r recent_rate` in 1981--2025, indicating clear acceleration. The random walk plus noise model is preferred over local linear trend alternatives by AIC, and its residuals show that short-run monthly autocorrelation remains---a natural motivation for more structured seasonal DLMs.

For the GHCN daily data, the bivariate DLM with unrestricted $W$ (Model 2) is strongly preferred by AIC, revealing that the latent temperature levels at the two Maine stations co-evolve with near-unity correlation. The spatially structured Model 3 provides a geographically interpretable alternative: its estimated decay parameter $\hat\phi = `r phi_m3`$ confirms that temperature trends are effectively coherent across the $\approx 270$ km separating the two stations, at only a modest cost in likelihood. Together, the two analyses demonstrate that Dynamic Linear Models provide a coherent and flexible framework for climate time series: they accommodate non-stationarity, propagate uncertainty through latent states, and extend naturally from univariate trend estimation to multivariate spatial modelling within the same inferential machinery. A VAR(1) benchmark confirms that the main residual predictive gap of the random walk specification is short-run AR(1) persistence, pointing to state-space models with autoregressive observation errors as a natural next step. An optional spatial seasonal DLM (Model 4) estimated on raw TMAX corroborates the main findings, confirming that the seasonal pre-adjustment adopted in Models 1--3 is adequate and that spatial coherence between the two stations holds regardless of the modelling approach.
